summary: Weekly POC check-in focusing on latency tuning for chat streaming. Reviewed TTFT regressions, sequence-length distributions, kernel choices and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed on targeted streaming test run, shared perf spreadsheet update, and provisioning dedicated test VPC for final latency tests.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We got about 45 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Sara Li: Sara here.
[00:08] Tom Reyes: Tom, on platform.
[00:10] Priya Kapoor: Priya, SRE.
[00:12] Marcus Voss: Marcus, ML infra.
[00:15] Jon Kim: Jon from Redwood, SE.
[00:17] Maya Patel: Cool. Agenda: quick check on last week's items, dive into TTFT numbers, streaming experiments, kernel choices, then agree next steps.
[00:28] Sara Li: Sounds good. We had the spike mid-week, curious what you found.
[00:33] Jon Kim: Yeah so we looked at the traces you shared. Two things jumped out: first, the cold KV cache on your deduped traffic caused extra decode time for first token, and second, interactions where you force long context (2k+ tokens) push kernel selection into slower paths.
[00:52] Tom Reyes: When you say slower paths, you mean falling back from the fused attention kernel?
[00:56] Jon Kim: Exactly, the runtime picks a more general kernel for >1024 seq on the current model config, which increases latency per token and affects TTFT because the model needs to do a couple key ops before streaming starts.
[01:08] Maya Patel: Quick question — are we sure it's kernel selection and not just provisioning? Tom, are your test nodes single-A100 or mixed?
[01:17] Tom Reyes: We're on mixed infra in the lab: mostly A100-80GB but a couple H100s in another pool. For the POC we pointed traffic at an A100 cluster.
[01:25] Jon Kim: That makes sense. A100 with the current NVF kernel set will do fine under 1024, but for 2k and above it switches and we see 20-30% slower iteration. H100 shows better perf for long context due to improved fp16 kernels.
[01:39] Priya Kapoor: Our distribution: 78% of queries are short (<256 tokens), 18% are medium (256-1024), and 4% are long (>1024). Does that change recommendations?
[01:48] Jon Kim: Yes — given your mix, optimising TTFT for short/medium is highest impact. For TTFT we can do three levers: prefix caching (your repeated user prompts), streaming chunk size tuning, and ensuring the model warms KV cache for the hot user flows.
[02:04] Marcus Voss: On prefix caching — how stateful is that? We're nervous about PII in cache.
[02:09] Jon Kim: Good call. Cache can be scoped per user-session and encrypted at rest. Redwood supports KMS-backed encryption for cache material and you can set TTLs or disable caching for sensitive routes.
[02:19] Sara Li: We need to check with privacy team — but sounds promising.
[02:22] Maya Patel: On streaming, we ran baseline numbers last week — overall TTFT was 280ms median but tails at 900ms. We pushed a micro-benchmark with 64B chunk streaming and saw small improvements but not consistent. Jon, did you replicate?
[02:36] Jon Kim: I reran with the provided traces. Streaming chunk size matters: too small and you pay more RPC overhead; too big and first token waits longer. For your workload a 128B-256B chunk hits a sweet spot. Also enabling early decoding on the runtime (we call early token flush) reduces TTFT for the first chunk.
[02:54] Tom Reyes: Is early token flush something we can toggle per route?
[02:57] Jon Kim: Yes, per-route setting in the Redwood config. We can enable it for chat routes and disable for other endpoints.
[03:03] Priya Kapoor: What about batching — we saw Redwood's suggestion to cap batch size to protect latency. Any numbers?
[03:09] Jon Kim: For your POC we suggest a dynamic batch cap of 8 for short requests and up to 32 for medium during off-peak; the runtime's batching policy can be workload aware so it won't batch across a route that's on low latency SLO.
[03:22] Sara Li: You mentioned kernel selection earlier — can you elaborate on the quantization tradeoffs? Our compliance team prefers deterministic outputs.
[03:29] Jon Kim: Quantization helps cost and sometimes perf for medium/long sequences, but it can slightly change output distribution — usually subtle. If determinism is critical, we recommend int8 with calibration and a holdout eval set to compare regressions. For strict determinism you'd run fp16 on H100 / A100 and rely on kernel-level optimizations instead of quant.
[03:48] Marcus Voss: So the pragmatic plan: keep production on hosted fp16 for now, test int8 with quant calibrations in a staging dedicated pool and compare eval metrics.
[03:57] Maya Patel: Yep that's what I was thinking. We also suggested a dedicated test VPC so you can run H100 lanes and A100 lanes and compare TTFT and full-latency. Tom, you ok to spin that up?
[04:07] Tom Reyes: Yes, I can provision a dedicated VPC in our project. I need the test instance specs and creds.
[04:12] Jon Kim: I'll put an infra manifest in the docs link after the call. For the benchmarks we want: 1) streaming TTFT with 1k requests across your short/medium/long split, 2) single-request cold start times, 3) throughput under a 95th percentile latency cap.
[04:26] Sara Li: For the streaming TTFT test, what's the expected run time?
[04:29] Jon Kim: With parallel workers it should finish in ~30 minutes for 1k requests, logs will be a few MB — we'll aggregate traces.
[04:36] Priya Kapoor: Any special logging I should enable? We currently do minimal app-level tracing.
[04:41] Jon Kim: Enable full runtime tracing for a 30-minute window, especially kernel selection flags and cache hit/miss counters. We'll give you a command to pull the trace bundle. Also enable per-request header pass-through so we can correlate session IDs.
[04:56] Maya Patel: Side note — we saw a few requests fall back to a smaller model variant during congestion. That's expected but need to ensure graceful degradation isn't changing outputs too much.
[05:05] Marcus Voss: Which fallback does Redwood use by default?
[05:08] Jon Kim: Policy is configurable — you can prefer latency-preserving fallback (smaller model with similar top-k) or throughput-preserving. We recommend latency-preserving fallback with A/B checks in the eval harness.
[05:18] Tom Reyes: On cost — do you have ballpark numbers for streaming with warm cache vs cold?
[05:22] Maya Patel: I have a spreadsheet but will update with our new kernel numbers. Cold runs look about 1.7x the token cost vs warm cache for your model; warm streaming is much cheaper.
[05:31] Sara Li: Ok that helps our procurement folks.
[05:34] Jon Kim: One more thing — for TTFT improvement we can also try pre-warming on expected high-value users. Redwood supports scheduled warmers that call the model with a pinned prefix to warm the KV cache for a user segment.
[05:46] Priya Kapoor: That might be helpful for our VIP flows. We'll need to audit for PII though.
[05:50] Maya Patel: Agreed.
[05:52] Jon Kim: Alright, next steps recap: Maya will share an updated perf spreadsheet + recommended kernel/quant profiles; Jon will run the streaming TTFT experiments and upload traces; Tom will provision the dedicated test VPC and give creds; we'll reconvene after results.
[06:09] Sara Li: Can we also get the security docs? We have a SOC2 review next month.
[06:14] Maya Patel: Yes I'll drop SOC2 + architecture + KMS notes.
[06:17] Tom Reyes: One last question — latency SLAs: do you have out-of-box SLO templates?
[06:21] Jon Kim: We do — per-route latency SLO templates and alerting integrations. We'll attach a suggested SLO for chat routes (p50 150ms, p95 350ms for TTFT target) and you can tune from there.
[06:34] Maya Patel: Great. Anything else?
[06:36] Sara Li: No, appreciate it.
[06:38] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll send notes and action items.
[06:41] Jon Kim: Thanks.
[06:43] End of recording.

Notes: transcript contains occasional transcription errors (e.g., "KV cash" in some auto-notes), speaker timestamps at ~1 min intervals to mimic Fireflies export. Links shared: perf spreadsheet (link redacted), infra manifest (link redacted), SOC2 pack (link redacted).
